# Implementation of hybrid simulation training to promote collective and self-efficacy in medical students: a two-pronged approach

**Authors:** Calvin Yuk Wang Tam; John Ian Wilzon T. Dizon; Simon Wai Ching Sin; Gloria Kai Yan Tang; Victor Yuk Wah Lai; Yvonne Yin Wong; Fraide A. Ganotice; Pauline Yeung Ng

**Affiliations:** aCritical Care Medicine Unit, School of Clinical Medicine, LKS Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong Island, HKSAR | bBau Institute of Medical and Health Sciences Education, LKS Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong Island, HKSAR | cHKU Health System Clinical Center, LKS Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pok Fu Lam, Hong Kong Island, HKSAR

## Abstract

Simulation-based training (SBT) is an integral and indispensable component of medical and healthcare education, especially pertinent in acute care. Conventional forms of SBT in acute care primarily involve manikins or task trainers, which are either costly or too task-specific. Recent innovations in virtual patient simulation software (VPS) invites the opportunity for conjoined use with basic manikins, creating a hybrid model for acute-care teaching. This study aimed to: ① Assess the impact of hybrid simulation teaching on the collective efficacy (CE) and self-efficacy (SE) of medical students, and ② evaluate psychometric measurement scales within the simulation context.

A prospective cross-sectional cohort study was conducted between 22 September 2023, and 19 December 2023. Fifth year medical students in an undergraduate medicine program underwent hybrid SBT, incorporating VPS and basic manikin within two separate clinical scenarios. Primary outcome of CE and SE was measured using adapted versions of the Perceived Collective Efficacy (PCE) scale and Motivational Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ). Both scales were distributed to students before and after undergoing hybrid SBT.

Data from 94 students were available for pairwise testing. Significant improvements were observed in the CE and SE of students after undergoing hybrid SBT [CE: (12.16 ± 3.86 vs 15.42 ± 2.87); p < 0.001]; [SE: 24(23–32) vs 32(28–34); p < 0.001]. Scale evaluation of Perceived Collective Efficacy (PCE) and Motivational Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) revealed good scale Cronbach α scores [PCE: pretest α = 0.929; posttest α = 0.914]; [MSLQ: pretest α = 0.971.; posttest α = 0.968].

Hybrid SBT facilitated by virtual patient simulator and basic manikin provides a moderate-cost and adaptable approach which positively impacted the CE and SE of medical students. As software development readily adapts in providing point-of-care learner feedback, hybrid SBT should become more widely implemented to fully harness its potential.

## Abstract

This study demonstrates that hybrid simulation-based training can enhance both self-efficacy and collective efficacy among medical students, providing evidence that this cost-effective approach can foster critical psychological attributes linked to better team collaboration and clinical performance.By combining virtual patient simulations with basic manikin, this study supports the potential hybrid simulation as a scalable, adaptable and more accessible teaching method for enhancing essential medical competencies.The study also validates the use of adapted scales for measuring collective and self-efficacy in medical education, paving the way for more widespread use of these tools in evaluating simulation-based training.

## Introduction

Since the revolutionary inception of the Resusci Anne and the Harvey Simulator in the 1960s, simulation-based training (SBT) has become an integral and indispensable component of healthcare education [1–7]. At its core, continued prevalence of SBT in modern healthcare is attributed to its effectiveness in providing hands-on experience to students without compromising patient care, providing learners a risk-free platform for repeated practices in safe and controlled environments [1–3]. These simulators have laid the foundation for training in healthcare practices, everchanging to meet the dynamic needs of the industry. Notable instances of dynamic adaptations include standardized simulation training modality incorporating basic manikin with simulated patient scenarios, like those seen in procedural protocols including basic life support (BLS) and advanced cardiovascular support (ACLS).

As of current, a variety of simulator modalities are implemented within medical and healthcare education [1,2,8–13], including manikin simulators, task trainers, virtual reality and standardized patients. With a wide array of simulators to pick and choose from, a pressing dilemma is presented: ‘How can we effectively consolidate the complex management of a patient into one intricate bundle?’. This is where hybrid SBT models become pertinent, offering unique properties that offset the limitations posed by singular model approach. The hybrid model we posit in this study includes a combination of basic task trainer manikin and virtual patient simulation (VPS) in a cohort of Asian medical students.

When designing SBT, one concept that often emerges is that of fidelity. In the context of our study, fidelity is defined according to Hamstra et al. which stratifies fidelity into two dimensions: (i) physical resemblance – characterized by the tactile, visual, auditory and olfactory appearance of the simulator relative to the simulation concept in mind; and (ii) functional task alignment – the simulator’s functional property in alignment with the learning objectives at hand [5,14–16].

This distinction is crucial in defining the proposed hybrid SBT model, as unequivocal interpretations of ‘high-fidelity’ in wider literature complicate model selection, particularly in resource-limited settings [8–13]. For instance, while a ‘high-fidelity’ manikin realistically simulating the physical resemblance and haemodynamics of a patient may be desirable, they often incur high costs, require extensive preparation and lack flexibility in scenario adaptation [15–18]. Conversely, ‘low-fidelity’ basic manikins including those used in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) training may not realistically depict the physical appearance of a patient, but can just as effectively facilitate functional alignment with tasks expected in CPR training (e.g. compression rhythm and timing mastery) at much lower costs and requirements in trainer preparation [19,20]. Furthermore, by incorporating elements of VPS into a model with basic task trainer manikin, we potentiate effects of both modalities by generating a logistically sound and feasible platform with elements of psychological benefits of enhanced engagement through the incorporation of immediate feedback and student tailoring.

Other drawbacks of high-fidelity manikin simulation include the need for extra staff to operate control panels and the additional training needed to respond and adapt to unexpected learner decisions. Furthermore, high-fidelity simulation also incurs high costs ranging from equipment, extra personnel and time required to train the trainer. Our proposed hybrid SBT model aims to enhance task-alignment of a standalone ‘low-fidelity’ CPR manikin by incorporating interactive elements seen in VPS, of which comes pre-programmed with patient scenarios and emulated haemodynamics. In doing so, this substitutes physical exam findings and other clinical information to be relayed through a high-fidelity manikin. The result is an adaptable, cost effective and effort efficient model alternative to conventional standalone high-fidelity manikin (Supplement S1) [21,22]. It is for these positive qualities and the team-based environment that hybrid SBT fosters which warrants further investigation.

To our knowledge, literature surrounding the combination of virtual-based education and traditional manikin-based training has not been extensively researched in the context of medical students, particularly with their effects on collective and self-efficacy. Despite the lower costs, versatility and Extant literature have mostly explored standalone modalities (e.g. VPS or ‘High-fidelity’ manikins) with respect to learner knowledge, competency, or during clinical examinations [1,2,6,7,14]. However, hybrid modalities (or ‘medium fidelity’ simulations) and their effects on CE and SE within Asian medical students have not been thoroughly examined. As such, we hypothesize that a hybrid learning modality combining VPS and basic task trainer manikins can positively impact CE and SE in medical students much the same way that ‘high-fidelity’ simulator modalities can in the context of acute patient care.

In light of these knowledge gaps, the aims and objectives of our study were to therefore: ① Evaluate the effects of hybrid SBT on the CE and SE of clinical year medical students; and ② validate scales for use in measuring collective and self-efficacy in the context of medical simulation education.

## Materials and methods

This study aimed to explore the impact of hybrid SBT on the CE and SE of fifth-year medical students at the University of Hong Kong. A cross-sectional cohort design was employed, conducted during the first semester of the 2023–2024 academic year, with students enrolled in mandatory critical care simulation sessions. Ethical approval for the study was granted by the HKU/HA HKW Institutional Review Board (IRB) in September 2023 (Reference number UW23-410). The following sections outline the study design, participant recruitment, data collection procedures and data analysis methods used to investigate the effects of hybrid SBT on student’s CE and SE.

### Study design and setting

Hybrid SBT was first implemented into the medical curricula. In the local study setting of Hong Kong, the first semester comprises the months of September to December. We opted for a cross-sectional cohort design as we aimed to recruit as many participants as possible to adequately power our study for hypothesis generation. The design choice was appropriate in evaluating changes in CE and SE arising immediately from the hybrid simulation model. Furthermore, as we did not provide any incentives for the participants, a cross-sectional design would eliminate attrition issues conventionally seen in longitudinal studies.

The fifth-year medical students sampled within our study are representative of medical students in the middle of their clinical clerkships, both locally and beyond Hong Kong. As such, all fifth-year medical students rotating through their ICU clerkships were approached and offered recruitment during the first semester. This study took place 22 September and 19 December 2023, at The University of Hong Kong. All participants were provided two separate informed consent sheets on the pre- and post-tests through written or digital means.

Inclusion criteria were ① all fifth-year undergraduate medical students, ② rotating through their ICU clerkship who, ③ consented to participation. As part of curriculum renewal efforts, all fifth-year medical students at the institution were the first cohort to participate in a newly established mandatory critical care simulation program during the 2023–2024 semester. This cohort was therefore selected through convenience sampling on practical grounds.

Exclusion criteria were fifth-year medical students who were involved in the pilot trials of the SBT, students with missing data from either the pre- or post SBT survey, and students who arrived late for the SBT. The study key criterion for missing data included either missing pre- or post-test scores. As the participant identification was dependent on de-identified self-reported initials, matching pre- and post- results depended on consistent reporting of student initials. Late participants also increased the margin for missing data, as the concurrent scheduling of the study with SBT sessions would cause them to miss the pretest but maintain eligibility to consent for the post-test. The full trial protocol is enclosed within Appendix 1.

### Samples and participants

The objective of the study was to examine the effectiveness of hybrid SBT on self-efficacy and collective efficacy of students undergoing training in critical care medicine. A total of 137 fifth-year medical students were eligible for enrolment. After excluding 10 students due to lack of consent and 33 students due to incomplete data, a total of 94 students had identifiable data to enable pairwise testing (Figure 1).

### Study conceptual framework

Traditionally, research on SBT within medical education has heavily emphasized clinical skills, problem-based learning, or academic excellence as outcomes of interest [1,2,13]. While these performative domains certainly do serve as predictive outcomes on academic performance [13], burgeoning strides are being made towards the induction of alternative, holistic learning attitudes into learner. Some notable instances of these learning attitudes include collective efficacy (CE) and self-efficacy (SE) [23–28], both of which emerge from and play a central theme in Bandura’s Self-Efficacy Theory (1997) and Social Cognitive Theory (2001).

To elucidate further, CE is an emergent group property resulting from the efforts of a team rather than from a single individual. CE represents a group’s shared belief in their conjoint efforts to organize and execute courses of actions required to accomplish specific tasks, rather than each individual [29–31]. Previous studies report improved CE being linked with key psychological outcomes, including increased levels of team effort, improved perseverance in face of adversity and increased motivation. Attitudes such as motivation are posited to increase due to belief that individuals within a team have little incentive to act unless they perceive their actions to produce desirable results [23,31–34]. Consequently, it is the sum of these behaviours and attitudes that predict future performance in a group-based healthcare setting [23,24,32,33], subsequently translating into positive clinical outcomes including reduction in clinical near misses, improved patient outcomes and fostering constructive communication between peers [23,34].

Analogous to CE is its individualistic counterpart SE. Distinctively, SE emphasizes on an individual’s belief in themselves to organize and execute actions to achieve attainment in specific tasks [29,30,35,36]. Furthermore, SE should also be distinguished from other similar concepts like self-esteem and self-confidence, as SE is more context-dependent and strongly associated with future performance. In contrast, self-esteem and self-confidence present as broader and generalized behaviours that do not directly associate with future performance [26,29]. Much like CE, higher levels of SE attainment are associated with salubrious outcomes within an individual, including learning engagement, increased motivation and academic success among medical students [27–29,37,38]. There are posited to be several sources of stimuli inducted into learners that drive attitudinal behaviours and elicit positive outcomes when performing specific tasks. These sources include verbal persuasion, vicarious experiences, emotional arousal and task accomplishment [29,35,36].

Relevant instances of stimuli being applied into practice include standardized life support algorithms like Basic Life Support. BLS programs offer learners the opportunity to freely practice fundamental lifesaving skills in high-stake and controlled environments. By repeatedly practicing compressions in these simulated environments, learners gradually buildup mastery experiences through repeated task accomplishments. This study hopes to extend the abovementioned frameworks onto hybrid SBT, demonstrating it an adequate driver for instilling mastery experiences and vicarious experiences onto students.

### Study materials

The setup for hybrid SBT included a simple bedside environment with one basic CPR manikin and an interactive display monitor (Figure 2). The display was used to project the VPS software, BodyInteract™, which students were able to interact through. Teaching case scenarios were selected based on availability within the software, supplemented with the manikin. We selected cases based on clinical competencies expected of a fifth-year medical student within the institution. Additional equipment used in both scenarios included simple airway devices (e.g. nasal cannula and non-rebreather masks), haemodynamic monitoring devices (e.g. blood pressure machines), mock intravenous medications and cannulations (e.g. central lines).

The first case presented a patient with an intracranial haemorrhage to address the systematic approach in assessing an unconscious patient. Key learning objectives from the scenario were ① assessment recognition of an unstable patient via a systematic ABCDE (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure) approach, ② differential diagnosis of unconsciousness and ③ basic airway management (e.g. use of nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal airway adjuncts). This case was selected as first in order according to the simpler management expected from students.

The second case featured a patient with sepsis secondary to pneumonia, which aimed to address the systematic approach in assessing and managing a patient with sepsis. Key learning objectives from second case were ① identification and diagnosis of septic shock, ② implementation and resuscitation of the virtual patient through the sepsis-1-hour bundle according to the surviving sepsis campaign guidelines [39]. This case scenario was selected due to the prevalence of the disease pathology within critical care and also due to the increased complexity to offset for potential baseline advantages gained in the observer role during the first scenario. After cycling through both were roughly 10 min long and aimed to reinforce the key learning objectives of the case, and address any management plans the students may have overlooked.

As we aimed to better deduce the learning affects of students, the teaching clinician and simulation facilitator would purposively foster a mastery-oriented climate where participants would be encouraged cooperate among peers, reinforce personal goal improvements and emphasize mistake-making as part of the process in our controlled hybrid SBT environment. Consequently, we did not seek to proactively assess or grade student competency or performance for the intents of the study. We ascertained that in acute-care practice, a predominantly performance-oriented motivational climate would result in intra-team member rivalry, unequal recognition among peers and undermine psychological safety of participants in fear of reprimand for speaking up [40–43], traits of which we perceive as detrimental in team-based approaches during acute-care management.

Each SBT session included 10 students. Five medical students would actively participate in team-based management, whereas the other five students would observe and record actions undertaken by the participating team. Two members of staff were actively engaged in SBT, including a teaching clinician and a simulation facilitator. Main roles and responsibilities of the teaching clinician included delivering key learning objectives and providing post-scenario debriefs. The clinician would adopt a situational leadership approach [44], offering students direction and guidance as needed.

The simulation facilitator was responsible for bridging the gap between the manikin and VPS. They would mirror physical exams performed on the manikin to the VPS and select management plans on the VPS based on group decisions. The results of student actions are relayed as real-time feedback on the VPS, such as the virtual patient’s condition improving or deteriorating based on the adequacy of treatment provided. All staff involved received brief training on the VPS and scenarios prior to the sessions, which is supplemented by a tutor guide (See Appendix 2a, 2b and 2c in the Supplement). Development of simulation-based scenarios were based on Kolb’s experimental learning theory [45], covering aspects of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization and active experimentation. The surveys scales used were reviewed by two independent content experts for relevance to scenario content and learning objectives.

### Measurement tools

#### Collective efficacy (CE)

CE was measured using the four-item Perceived Collective Efficacy (PCE) Likert scale, adapted from the General Self Efficacy Scale developed by Schwarzer (1995) [46] and modified by Salanova [47] for work groups. This scale has been validated in cohorts of Hong Kong undergraduate and medical students [23,46]. It is due to this previous validation in a similar cohort that we have subsequently adapted the PCE items to our hybrid SBT context to more accurately measure CE in acute/critical care settings. For instance, the original item, ‘My group is able to solve difficult tasks if we invest the necessary effort’, was adapted to ‘My group is able to manage a critically ill patient if we invest the necessary effort’. Responses were scored on a five-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

#### Self-efficacy (SE)

Measurements for SE were conducted using an eight-item adapted subscale based on the original Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) SE for learning and performance subscale [48,49]. MSLQ has been previously validated and used in measuring SE of Western and Asian medical students in problem-based learning environments [50,51]. We have subsequently adapted the MSLQ’s self-efficacy for learning and performance subscale items to our hybrid SBT context to more accurately measure SE in acute/critical care settings. For example, the item from the original self-efficacy for learning and performance subscale, ‘I am confident I can understand the basic concepts taught in this course’, was adapted to ‘I am confident I can/will understand the basic concepts in the explored topic areas (e.g. managing critically ill patients’. Each item was scored on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

#### Subgroup measures

Sub-group analysis of differences between male and female were conducted with the rationale of uncovering underlying social dynamics between differences in gender and their respective effects on student CE/SE expectations within simulation [52]. Better understanding gender dynamics and social influences on CE/SE will aid in establishing learner centred teaching approaches.

As the medical syllabus within the local context was offered as an undergraduate route, differences in undergraduates vs postgraduates were also selected as a sub-group of interest. We sought to determine whether mature postgraduate students would attain higher CE/SE scores compared to their undergraduate counterparts at baseline and after completing hybrid SBT.

#### Secondary outcome

Secondary outcome measures to evaluate the adapted CE and SE scales in the context of SBT were defined according to the recommendations proposed by Boateng et al. and Dima [53,54]. Boateng et al. posits that scale development and validation are split into three phases of item development, scale development and scale evaluation. For the purposes of this study, we aimed to evaluate preexisting scales in the context of our study population and hybrid SBT activity. To achieve this, we conducted confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) of a single-factor model. Because latent variables such as CE and SE cannot be tangibly observed, measurements of these variables become implausible. Therefore, strategies are needed operationally define latent variables such that they can represent a behaviour or outcome of interest. It is for this reason that CFA is important, as it determines scale validity by psychometrically testing the systematic fit of a specified model by determining the relationship between observable variables (e.g. items within the scale) and latent constructs (e.g. collective efficacy). In doing so, we ensure our scale accurately and appropriately measures the intended latent construct, thus enabling us to draw reliable conclusions on the effect of intervention through data [23,55,56]. Since the scales we adapted for use had already been previously validated in a cohort of medical students in Hong Kong [23,24], we did not allocate items of the scale to be freely estimated as expected in exploratory factor analysis, and sought only to ascertain if data we collected fit the a priori model. Scale evaluation was therefore divided into two sections: ① Tests of dimensionality – measured CFA; and ② Tests of reliability – measured through Cronbach’s α.

### Data collection procedures

A survey containing 12 items from the PCE and MSLQ scales was administered by the simulation facilitator to the students before and after the simulation teaching activity to evaluate student perceived CE and SE. The complete survey is enclosed within Appendix 3a and 3b. The flow of the hybrid simulation training and survey/pre-posttest administration is shown in Figure 3. During each SBT session, the simulation facilitator and administrative staff at the venue would share an online link to the pre-course survey shortly after the students arrive for session registration.

A maximum of 10 min was allocated for students to complete the survey prior to an introductory video on VPS based training being played. When all students have undergone their respective session and debrief, the simulation facilitator would be tasked with providing another online link to the post-course survey. To minimize potential occurrences of coercion, participation was made entirely voluntary and participant anonymity was preserved by only requiring participants to declare their initials. Respondents were also given the option to respond to the surveys away from the simulation room to mitigate the confounding effects of environmental pressures on response.

### Data analysis

Student demographics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Categorical data was presented as frequencies with percentages. Normally distributed continuous variables were presented as means with standard deviations, whereas non-normally distributed continuous variables were depicted and expressed as medians with interquartile ranges. To justify the sample size for our study cohort, we obtained preliminary data from a pilot trial involving 18 volunteer fifth-year medical students. As these students would undergo the same interventions and stimuli, they would be excluded from the main study. Paired continuous variables were obtained, with the mean differences and standard deviations used to calculate preliminary effect and sample size. Assuming an α error of 0.05 and 1-β error of 0.8, preliminary effect sizes obtained in the pilot CE and SE results were d = 0.636 and d = 0.919 respectively, indicating an estimated sample size of at least n = 22 for detecting a statistically significant difference in CE and n = 12 in SE.

Shapiro-Wilk (SW) tests were used to assess data distribution [57,58]. Pre- and post-test CE scores were normally distributed, therefore paired samples t-tests were used for CE analysis. Underlying assumptions for t-tests SE pretest scores were non-normally distributed, therefore necessitating Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests for analysis (Supplement S2). The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank tests are for paired and non-normally distributed data that assumes independence between pairs and symmetrical distribution of differences between groups. Box-and-whisker plots would be used to visually display the median (Q2), lower quartile (Q1), third quartile (Q3) and outliers for CE and SE scores of the primary outcome. Effect sizes of normally distributed results were reported using Cohen’s d while effect sizes of non-normally distributed results were reported using rank biserial correlation, a simple difference formula used in computing effect sizes for Mann Whitney U in providing insight into correlations [59].

Exploratory sub-group analyses of gender differences and undergraduate vs postgraduate differences were conducted using independent two-samples t-tests for normally distributed continuous variables, and Mann-Whitney U tests for non-normally distributed continuous variables (Supplement S3). Mann-Whitney U tests are for non-normally distributed data that are independent of each other between groups, the assumption of symmetrical distribution of differences still hold [60].

The assumptions of confirmatory factory analyses are correct model specification, random sampling, adequate sample size, multivariate normal distribution and linearity between observed and latent variables. Cronbach’s α analyses measure how closely related and consistent a set of survey items are by comparing the amount of shared variance. Data management and statistical analysis were conducted using Stata-18 software (StataCorp LP), with a two-tailed statistical significance of p < 0.05 [61].

For our secondary outcome of validating scale acceptability, we conducted CFA [53,54] to assess and determine the suitability of our adapted scale and the original a priori factor structures in our current sample. Results from CFA include chi-square test of exact fit, degrees of freedom, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA ≤ 0.06), Tucker Lewis Index (TLI ≥ 0.95), comparative fit index (CFI ≥ 0.95) and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR ≤ 0.08) [53,62]. Reliability tests were performed using Cronbach’s α in both CE and SE scales in pretest and posttest, as well as the Corrected item-total correlations and Cronbach’s α if item is deleted. Statistical analysis of secondary outcomes were performed on IBM SPSS Statistics Version 29.0.2.0 [63] and IBM SPSS AMOS 28 Graphics for scale validation [64]. All p values obtained were two-tailed, with values less than 0.05 indicating statistical significance.

## Results

The purpose of this study was to examine the impact of hybrid SBT on CE and SE among fifth-year medical students. Results from the analysis are presented below, starting with primary outcomes, followed by subgroup analyses, secondary outcomes and participant feedback.

### Primary outcome

#### Impact of hybrid SBT on CE and SE

In our primary outcome, CE scores were paired and normally distributed. Therefore, paired t-tests were employed, with effect sizes reported as Cohen’s d. For analysis of paired independent non-normally distributed SE scores, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Tests were employed for, with effect size reported using rank biserial correlations.

Students reported significantly lower CE scores at baseline as compared to posttest. However, after progressing through hybrid SBT their CE scores significantly increased, which is further evidenced by means and standard deviations of their pretest vs posttest CE scores (12.16 ± 3.859 vs 15.42 ± 2.87, p < 0.001) Large effect size (d = 0.811) suggests that the improvements are of practical significance after undergoing hybrid SBT.

A similar trend was observed in the SE of students, where their self-perceived SE at baseline was significantly lower, but would subsequently be improved after undergoing hybrid SBT as evidenced by the median of their pretest vs posttest SE scores (24, 23–32, vs 32, 28–34, p < 0.001). A medium to moderate effect size (rpb = 0.461) suggests that differences were practical and substantial after undergoing hybrid SBT. Detailed test results are shown in Tables 2 and 3 and Figure 4.

### Subgroup analyses

#### Gender differences in CE and SE

In our subgroup analyses of gender differences, CE scores were normally distributed. Therefore, paired t-tests were employed, with effect sizes reported as Cohen’s d. Contrarily, as SE scores were independent and non-normally distributed, Mann-Whitney U was employed, with effect size reported using rank biserial correlations.

### Anecdotal feedback

While we did not incorporate structured interviews or focus groups for thematic analysis in our study design, we included an open-ended comment section at the end of the posttest survey to obtain supplementary anecdotal feedback from participants regarding their perceptions of the activity. The open-ended comments revealed two recurrent themes: One respondent expressed that they ‘wanted mores scenarios, more sessions’, and another participant remarking that they ‘had a very nice tutor’. These observations could highlight potential considerations in future designs. Notably, the first theme may have indicated the participant’s desire for broadening the scenario scope and diversity, whereas the second theme warrants further exploration into how instructor variations may influence outcomes despite our standardized instructor guides.

To summarize our results, the primary outcome results in our study showed that our acute-care hybrid SBT model was able to increase the baseline CE and SE of fifth-year medical students. Additionally, while our subgroup analyses of gender differences revealed no differences in pretest and posttest CE between genders, pretest SE scores were higher in males compared to females. However, these gender differences were nullified in posttest SE. Our subgroup analyses between undergraduates and postgraduates also showed no discernible differences in CE and SE, both pretest and posttest. Finally, data we provide in our secondary outcome of CFA is satisfactory and within acceptable ranges, further supporting the validity and reliability of the adapted PCE and MSLQ scales in measuring CE and SE.

## Discussion

### Summary of main findings

In this study, we sought to achieve our two research objectives of ① evaluating the effects of hybrid SBT on the CE and SE of fifth-year medical students, and ② validate scales for use in measuring CE and SE in the context of critical care simulation. Results from our first research objective revealed that fifth-year medical students who partook in the hybrid SBT program had markedly improved posttest CE and SE scores as compared to their baseline, as evidenced by the large effect size of d = 0.81 in CE, and moderate effect size of rpb = 0.461 in SE. The secondary objective of scale validation was also achieved with satisfactory results obtained from the CFA, indicating that our adapted PCE and MSLQ scales used in our study cohort had good model fit to the data in line with the a priori models.

#### Clinical performance and patient outcomes

Although this study did not examine the direct effects of changes in CE or SE on learning goals or academic successes, the congruency of CE with positive team-based outcomes is well-documented. Within wider literature, higher CE scores have been linked with group-level psychological outcomes, including stronger team commitment, efforts and perseverance in the face of adversity. Subsequently, it is the translation of these traits into positive clinical outcomes in which we perceive its value in, such as reductions in clinical near misses, improved patient outcomes and fostering constructive communication between peers [23,34]. Similarly, higher SE scores were seen to correlate with improved individual-level outcomes within extant literature, including increased learning engagement, motivation and goal commitments. These constructs have also been shown to be positively associated with non-technical skills within clinical practice, notably improved communication and multidisciplinary collaboration, active participation and engagement between healthcare practitioners [27–29,37,38].

#### Summary of subgroup analysis

Subgroup analysis between male and female revealed that there was no statistically significant difference in CE at baseline and after intervention. However, gender differences in SE yielded unexpected findings, with females initially reporting lower baseline SE scores compared to males but subsequently equalizing with their male counterparts after undergoing hybrid SBT. Interestingly, our finding of lower baseline SE in females are consistent with results from the wider literature encompassing STEM and humanities [40,52,65–68]. One such instance is explored in a quantitative study by Stewart et al., where they examine whether SE varies by gender and STEM academic domains [68]. In their study, significantly higher baseline SE attainments were observed in males as compared to females at the beginning of their STEM courses. However, like the posttest results in our study, Stewart et al. notes that as students progressed from their introductory physics classes to advanced ones, SE was no longer moderated by gender. This common trend of SE plateauing was likely attributed to mastery experiences yielded from achieving favourable test results, being a more prominent favourable driver of academic SE than cultural imposition [68].

In contrast to the gender differences reported in STEM students, studies including medical students and healthcare professionals do not appear to reflect similar gender trends [25,28,66,69,70]. One instance is noted by Kubrusly et al., where they examine SE beliefs in medical students undergoing a hybrid medical course of problem-based learning and traditional teaching [70]. They conducted a cross-sectional study in Brazil, where they note that female students had higher SE attainments as compared to their male counterparts. Conversely, Wu et al. conducted a cross-sectional study where they sought to determine if SE differed based on gender as part of an outcome. Their study cohort consisted of 1,930 Chinese medical students ranging from Freshmen (year 1) to Seniors (year 4), of which 1,357 were female. The authors indicate no significant difference in SE attainments between males or females across all years [28].

To elucidate on our findings of low SE observed within female students, we turn to Hofstede’s (1993) theory on cross-cultural differences in SE [71,72]. Hofstede posits that six key factors influence perceived self-efficacy cross-culturally ― power distance, masculinity, individualism/collectivism, long-term orientation, uncertainty avoidance and indulgence/restraint. In our study, lower baseline reported in female students may be attributed to the cultural context of Hong Kong, characterized by traditional gender roles of masculinity, collectivism and uncertainty avoidance [72]. These traditional gender roles discourage women from assertive and risk-taking behaviour, inadvertently affecting communication or willingness to take on leadership roles, of which are heavily expected within medicine [71–73]. These cultural implications align with our findings, as female students initially showed lower SE compared to males but achieved parity after undertaking hybrid SBT. These insights suggest that cultural factors contribute the SE observed among female medical students in our study, however, further research exploring the underlying SE dynamics among female students in STEM and medical fields are required to deduce the interplay.

Analysis between undergraduates and postgraduates revealed that there was no statistically significant difference in CE and SE at baseline and after intervention. This finding was not in line with expectations in the program structure, as undergraduate students within the institution typically begin their studies at age 18 and reach their fifth year at age 22. Comparatively, postgraduate medical students would have to complete a minimum of a bachelor’s degree (3-year mode of study or above) to be eligible to enrol in medicine, with the youngest theoretical postgraduate student being age 25. Postgraduate students were therefore anticipated to show higher CE and SE due to their accrued academic and life experiences, whereas undergraduates, theorized to accrue fewer life experiences and curricular rigors, were expected to show lower CE and SE. However, this parity of CE and SE results between undergraduates and postgraduates after undergoing hybrid SBT could potentially be explained by cognitive biases such as Dunning-Kruger effect (DKE). DKE theory posits that novice, or inexperienced individuals overestimate their abilities whereas those with adequate skillset tend to underestimate their capabilities [74,75]. As there is a paucity in current literature regarding CE and SE between younger vs mature students, future studies may benefit by exploring effects of this phenomena in relation to hybrid SBT. Additionally, low statistical power from sample size may necessitate validation in larger future cohorts.

When compared with existing simulation studies in the field, our study focused mostly on the learning affects attributed to hybrid SBT modality which as an alternative traditional manikin-based simulation. In contrast, extant literature has mostly revolved around learner competency or knowledge as an outcome after undergoing standalone simulators [2,8–13]. This study therefore adds to the body of knowledge by providing more evidence for ① hybrid simulators as a tool for development in CE/SE, ② periodic baseline assessment of efficacies between male and female in medical education and ③ evidence-based validation and reliability tools for assessing student affects during simulation teaching.

### Hybrid SBT model

Our study showed that a hybrid SBT combination of basic manikins and VPS offers a cost effective, adaptable alternative to the traditional ‘high-fidelity’ manikins seen in the literature. By integrating components of cognitive and psychomotor skill development in the model, this provides an opportunity for students to safely manage a simulated patient in a high acuity setting, reinforcing clinical skills, procedural skills, reducing procedural errors, or improving speed of decision-making [1]. Additionally, the flexibility of the model enables scaling of scenarios to match expected competencies and learning outcomes across student year groups. For instance, preclinical third year students may benefit from simulation sessions involving history taking skills, differential diagnostics, or initial patient workup, whereas experienced sixth year (graduating year) students could be challenged with mixed sessions incorporating procedural tasks (e.g. blood-taking, intravenous access) in conjunction with the complete management of a patient’s journey. Furthermore, while the model focused primarily on medical students, scenarios offered by VPS software are expansive and include scenarios of different health sectors. Future comparisons of CE and SE disparities in allied health vs medical students may prove useful in curriculum designing, especially in knowing which cohort of students are more receptive to the intervention and allocating resources accordingly.

Compared to traditional SBT, the model reduces trainer commitment (‘train the trainer’) and offers extended case interchangeability through off-the-shelf VPS software. This is important to note, as within traditional SBT, patient actors, facilitators and instructors need to dedicate time and commitment in learning the content and script required for a clinical scenario. Although this is important for ensuring consistency, the process lacks case interchangeability and necessitates time commitment from trainers. The utility of off-the-shelf VPS software packages offer a broad selection of case scenarios which can be easily adapted to course-specific learning needs. Our findings therefore address the current limitations in medical simulation and provide a practical alternative framework for skill development. Future research should explore hybrid SBT’s long-term impact on clinical reasoning and its effectiveness in diverse multidisciplinary educational contexts (e.g. CE between nursing and medical students), or within rural settings.

### Scale evaluation of instruments

Scale evaluation of instruments used in assessing the CE and SE of students confirmed the dimensionality and reliability of the scores obtained. As scales are a measurement of latent and underlying constructs including behaviour and feelings, this cannot be assessed directly through single variable items. The current study findings highlighted that among a sample of Asian medical students, both the scales for CE (PCE) and SE (MSLQ) that were adapted for use in hybrid SBT in the context of critical care scenarios yielded acceptable internal consistencies (via Cronbach’s alpha) and good model fit to the data (via Confirmatory Factor Analysis). Such findings corroborate and extend results from previous studies citing the validity, reliability and utility of the PCE [23,46,47] and MSLQ [48,50,51] in measuring CE and SE among medical students.

We provide data to support more widespread and uniform use of these tools in the process of evaluating educational activities. Teachers and curriculum designers should aim to simultaneously address objectives of knowledge delivery, as well as fostering psychological attributes in medical students. These psychological dimensions range from self- and collective efficacy, motivation, confidence, teamwork and communication skills. To promote and gauge efficacy, the same dimensions should be repeatedly measured over time and across different training activities. The utility of these scales in the professional and subspecialty training of experienced healthcare providers could be explored in future cohorts, either as guide for curriculum development (e.g. longitudinal tracking of CE and SE in student cohorts), or as remediation strategies for underperforming students.

### Limitations

While the study provides valuable insight into the enhancement of CE and SE in the context of hybrid SBT for medical students, there were limitations and constraints that should be addressed to enhance the generalizability and interpretability of study findings.First, our preliminary sample size calculation suggested a minimum of n = 22 participants for an adequately powered study. While our study satisfied this preliminary requirement with a total of n = 94 samples, a small sample within our preliminary analysis may have inflated the effect size, nonetheless. Future studies could therefore aim for larger sample sizes to improve precision of results.Second, while we initially designed the study to be as deidentified as possible to protect student identity, this led to an unfortunate increase in unmatched samples (n = 33). To address the unexpectedly high number of unmatched samples, we included verbal instructions and reminders for students to keep consistent when reporting their initials. However, despite efforts, this may have still inadvertently reduced the power of our study in detecting significant differences. One positive prospect from this outcome was that the unmatched samples were lost at random, pointing towards non-informative missingness in follow-up data. The observable loss in posttest data can be attributed to the absence of grading for survey participation reducing incentivization to follow-up. Furthermore, as the study was wholly voluntary without monetary or academic incentives for participants, this may have further contributed to an increase in unmatched samples. As the unmatched samples were missing at random and unrelated to observable data, this is unlikely to contribute heavily to a skewed interpretation of the results. However, future considerations to improve this outcome would be the distribution of study codes assigned to each participant for use in their pre and posttests, rather than relying on subject self-selected initials.Third, while convenient, the cross-sectional nature limits the timepoints in which data was collected, and convenience sampling of participants in this study introduces potential confounding effects of selection bias in consenting students. Large-scale longitudinal studies could resolve generalizability concerns by examining residual effects of hybrid SBT on CE and SE at additional time points, enriching the data for robust comparisons between different simulator modalities (e.g. hybrid SBT vs standalone ‘high-fidelity’), especially the paucity of information regarding long-term retention of CE and SE in medical students within the wider literature. Regarding convenience sampling, traditional drawbacks attributed include reduced generalizability and selection bias, however by stratifying our homogenous sample of fifth-year medical students based on their demographics (e.g. male vs female), we mitigate some of these effects by providing insight into the nuanced influences of confounders through our subgroup analysis. Moreover, while the scales were psychometrically validated and reliable in the context of our study populace, there remains the possibility of response bias, especially considering the self-reporting measures we employed. However, the effects of this bias on student CE/SE scores may have been blunted to an extent, as we enabled students to anonymously report their results.Fourth, our cohort consisted only of fifth-year medical students. From an academic and clinical perspective, these students have gained a considerable amount of clinical insight and experience as compared to those in their preclinical years (MBBS third year and below). As such, the generalizability of these results in relation to medical students within their preclinical years remains unrefuted. While extant literature has not provided conclusive evidence of SE variations between different year groups, inferential data observed from STEM fieldFifth, occurrences of unforeseen software glitches and misrepresentation of clinical information could negatively influence the learning efficacy and attitudes of students, as majority of clinical reasoning were taught through VPS. An instance of software bugs/system error came in the form of a simulated patient with a recent history of cholecystectomy who still presented with gallbladder on a computed-tomography scan. Better bidirectional lines of communication should be established between software developers and instructors to ensure that content is both continually reviewed and updated.Sixth, when gathering data from participants, we focused primarily on the technical characteristics of participants as well as the adapted PCE and MSLQ scales. While we collected open-ended qualitative feedback from participants in the form of short comments, in retrospect, more forethought on gathering qualitative insights from participants and clinical instructors could have provided more anecdotal evidence to enrich our analysis of the hybrid SBT in terms of engagement, confidence and performance [76].Finally, at present, only generic and predetermined scenarios are offered by the software. Future integration of artificial intelligence to optimize virtual patient history taking could improve the rapport building between students and virtual patients. Additionally, providing options to customize VPS case scenarios to cater for diverse student populations with varying learning needs represents both a limitation and area for improvement.

### Implications for future research

First, in addition to quantitative analysis, future studies can consider incorporating the use of mixed-methods approach in analyzing quantitative scores alongside a qualitative thematic analysis of participant interviews. In doing so, we can provide a holistic overview of shared themes and perspectives among students, as well as in critically exploring enriching the robustness and rigour of data in deducing our hypothesis.

Second, while our research was inclusive of both undergraduate and postgraduate students, a more thorough exploration of CE and SE disparities in medical students across year of study may provide help tailor decision-making and identify appropriate student cohorts which may maximize efficacy development from hybrid SBT approaches. Specifically, if medical students within their clinical years were found to have smaller differences between their pre-posttest CE/SE scores than preclinical medical students after undergoing hybrid SBT, the simulator may be providing diminishing returns to the more experienced students in their clinical years and suggesting alternative interventions for fostering efficacies.

Third, our study has focused exclusively on hybrid SBT within the context of medical students. To enhance generalizability of benefits derived from the hybrid SBT design, future research should involve actively practicing providers and allied healthcare professionals within multidisciplinary teams. Such research would aid in ascertaining the efficaciousness and applicability of the hybrid model in fostering CE and SE among experienced learners across diverse disciplines. Furthermore, should the current hybrid SBT design be expanded to include students within allied health fields, the scenarios of present are not optimally tailored to the learning needs and competencies of allied health students, thereby necessitating exploration on optimal case customizations for each respective field. Potential research questions addressing these concerns might include an exploration of allied health student’s receptiveness towards tailored cases and assessing their adaptations to the scenarios in comparison to their medical student counterparts.

Third, the comparatively low-cost and high adaptability of the hybrid SBT approach would be most advantageous in resource-limited settings, particularly in institutions or departments with budget and personnel constraints who intend on training medical students and other healthcare students. Depending on the objectives of the training program, certain elements can be enhanced, such as the pairing of basic manikin with task trainer to facilitate the practice of blood-taking skills. The developers of virtual patient simulation software could consider incorporating short training seminars for potential users. A brief review of literature examining different simulator modalities in relation to cost and effort investment was conducted. We suggest that a thorough and rigourous exploration and analysis on the return-on-investment between traditional simulation modalities compared to a hybrid SBT model.

Finally, our research also provides a general flow of consideration for future researchers with interest in other populations or outcome measures necessitating multi-factor or hierarchical model analysis of CE and SE.

### Implications for clinical practice

First, improvements in CE and SE as observed in the literature have been associated with better clinical performance and longstanding retention in medical training

Second, previous studies have shown that by fostering a climate which champions mastery-oriented experiences over performance-oriented experiences, learners become increasingly self-regulated and motivated in setting actionable and SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound) [77]. In doing so, this sets up the learner to continuously adapt and overcome similar adversities when undergoing other tasks [23,29,38]. These qualities are posited to factor in the academic successes of students. Fostering development of CE and SE is an important process of empowering medical students to manage medical emergencies confidently and successfully.

Third, as the hybrid SBT model we propose is versatile and scalable in design, the intents and purposes of the setup can be extended beyond core curricula, but as a supplementary practice tool for medical specialty specific activities. Incorporation of a mastery-oriented climate combined with the versatility and scalability offered by hybrid SBT present feasible opportunities for focus groups or remediating medical students to practice in an environment that fosters self-regulation and self-mastery [41,78,79], rather than academic and performance oriented climate often seen within medical assessments and clerkships. By nurturing positive habits and attitudes towards topic areas students once perceived as troublesome, we can instil lifelong habits of self-initiated continuous professional development.

Finally, students identified with baseline deficits in CE/SE scores may potentially benefit from gender congruent role modelling by instructors or may benefit from a shared sense of accomplishment through completion of less challenging scenarios. Furthermore, students with higher baseline efficacies that do not change after intervention may also benefit from a wider breath of complex scenarios to limit test themselves. For future consideration during SBT, the use of successful role models and social support can be beneficial to demographic of participants during stepwise management of the patient in SBT. Clinical instructors running similar simulation models could potentiate their teaching by using these scales to assess student baseline SE and CE. Using such information in this manner could provide directed support to students with lower baseline scores.

In summary our study provides evidence for new directions which simulation modalities can be delivered in. We also provide logistic and psychological overview of the benefits of hybrid simulation modality as compared to ‘high-fidelity’ and other frequented platforms. Our study results also provide further clinical questions regarding cross-cultural differences in learning affects and potential strategies used to monitor and continuously assess CE and SE, potentially tailoring school curricula for specific learner needs.

## Conclusions

In this study, we have shown that a hybrid SBT model incorporating both basic manikin and VPS, is effective in improving the CE and SE of fifth-year medical students. Additionally, we also examined the validity and reliability of adapted PCE and MSLQ scales for assessing CE and SE within a hybrid training context. Complementing our study findings, a review of pertinent literature reveals that increased CE and SE are associated with improved team communication, learning engagement and patient outcomes. We also consider the confounding effects of student demographics, specifically differences in gender and distinction between undergraduate vs postgraduate students, thereby offering newer insights into gender-based disparities in SE.

In contrast to existing studies, our research differs in that we evaluated the efficaciousness of a relatively novel and moderately priced hybrid simulation modality in fostering learning affects within students, rather than a standalone high-fidelity manikin approach extensively reported in the wider literature. This hybrid SBT method therefore offers a valid alternative to our approach in simulation training, challenging the perception of high-fidelity manikin training as the gold standard. By diversifying the pool of options when designing simulation do we provide more flexible, scalable and tailored options for educators, thereby fostering a culture of accessibility within the wider simulation community.

However, it is also important to acknowledge that the study’s focus on a population fifth-year medical students may have hampered the generalizability and interpretability of the results, especially when applying our methods to medical students of varying demographics. Given that our study cohort primarily consisted of Asian medical students, potential discrepancies in CE and SE results may arise from cross-cultural dimensions, such as individualism and individualism as previously discussed. This cultural context may therefore render the results less generalizable in other study settings. Our study findings also provide further insight into cross-cultural implications on the self-efficacy of medical students, notably with our cohort of female students exhibiting lower baseline levels of SE than those reported in medical literature. Training of educators in our model required the elaboration of the main learning objectives and the flow of the simulation scenario in text, and one 2-hour session of environmental familiarization. Moreover, salient factors including instructor quality, environmental conditions and participant’s prior exposure to critical care practice may have influenced the outcomes of the study. Ensuring stringent control of these variables in future research efforts should be considered for a more robust interpretation of results.

Finally, as software development adapts more easily to local contexts and offers point-of-care learner feedback, hybrid SBT should be more widely implemented to fully harness its potential. Medical educators should continuously develop and adapt to the emerging scene of software-based tools to complement traditional simulation-based training, while adopting the validated PCE and MSLQ scales where necessary for objective quantification of CE and SE. These scales are indispensable tools to benchmark educational activities and should be used to identify subgroups of learners who may require additional and tailored support. In future research, it is worthwhile to explore advantages associated with hybrid SBT in relation with formal cost-effective analyses and in qualitative evaluation.
